v1-p1.V1-1-01:
Nibbānagāminipaṭipadā

The Practice Leading to Nibbāna — Volume I

Namo tassa bhagavato arahato sammāsambuddhassa.

Homage to the Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One.
v1-p1.V1-1-02:
The Great Homage — Homage to the Buddha

Munindakko yeko dayudayaruṇo ñāṇavitthiṇṇabimbo,
vineyyappāṇoghaṃ kamalakathitaṃ dhammaraṃsivarehi;
subodhesi suddhe tibhavakuhare byāpitakkittinañca,
tilokekacakkhuṃ dukhamasahānaṃ taṃ mahesiṃ namāmi.

I bow to that great seer, the sun who is lord of sages. His dawn is compassion and his vast disc is knowledge. With the excellent rays of the Dhamma he brought to full bloom the multitude of beings fit to be guided, likened to lotuses in the clear pool of the three realms of existence. His renown spread far. He is the sole eye of the three worlds and endures what is hard to endure.

Translator’s note
v1-p1.V1-1-03: Dayudayaruṇo — Having as his newly risen dawn the attainment of great compassion. Ñāṇavitthiṇṇabimbo — Having as his vast solar disc the knowledge of omniscience. Eko — Arising and appearing alone, without an equal in the ten thousand world systems. Yo munindakko — That sun who is lord of sages, the Buddha. Suddhe — Clear, pure, cool and limpid. Tibhavakuhare — In the lotus pool of the three realms of existence: sensual, fine-material and immaterial. Nibbattaṃ — Having arisen and grown through the impetus of kamma associated with the perfections. Kamalakathitaṃ — Called lotuses. Vineyyappāṇoghaṃ — The multitude of beings who may be led to liberation, the lotuses that are human beings, deities and brahmās. Dhammaraṃsivarehi — With the excellent rays of the Dhamma, his noble discourses that lead to the attainment of path and fruition and enable one to see Nibbāna. Subodhesi — He brought them to full bloom, enabling them to penetrate and see the Four Noble Truths.
v1-p1.V1-1-04: Byāpitakkittinañca — His renown was manifest throughout the ten thousand world systems, up to the brahmā realms, through his unsurpassed qualities of morality, concentration and wisdom. Tilokekacakkhuṃ — He is the sole eye of the three worlds, of brahmās, deities and human beings. Dukhamasahānaṃ — Like the great earth, he could endure what is hard to endure. Mahesiṃ — He sought and cultivated exceptional qualities: the aggregates of morality, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and knowledge and vision of liberation. Taṃ munindakkaṃ — That sun who is lord of sages, the Buddha. Ahaṃ — I, your disciple. Namāmi — With the three volitions of body, speech and mind, and with a clear, trusting heart, I respectfully lower myself, subdue pride and bow to you, venerable Buddha.

v1-pA.V1-A-01:
Introduction (Nidānakathā) — The Reasons for This Work

Namo tassa bhagavato arahato sammāsambuddhassa.

Homage to the Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One.

Nibbānagāminipaṭipadā — Volume I
v1-pA.V1-A-02:
Yaṃ passati na taṃ diṭṭhaṃ, yaṃ diṭṭhaṃ taṃ na passati; apassaṃ bajjhate mūḷho, bajjhamāno na muccati.

What one sees is not what should be seen. What should be seen, one does not see. Failing to see, the deluded one is bound. While bound, one does not gain release.1
v1-pA.V1-A-03: Loko — People who are blind in the eye of wisdom that penetrates ultimate reality. Yaṃ — Whatever man or woman. Passati — Sees mistakenly, taking what is seen for a man or a woman. Taṃ — That man or woman whom those blind in the eye of wisdom that penetrates ultimate reality mistakenly perceive. Diṭṭhaṃ — What truly ought to be seen and deserves to be seen with the eye of wisdom that penetrates ultimate reality. Na — Is not.
v1-pA.V1-A-04: Yaṃ — (a) Whatever visible form, (b) whatever collection of body parts beginning with head hair, or (c) whatever collection of great essentials and derived materiality. Diṭṭhaṃ — What the wise truly ought to see and what deserves to be seen with the eye of wisdom that penetrates ultimate reality.
v1-pA.V1-A-05: Taṃ — (a) That visible form, (b) that collection of body parts beginning with head hair, or (c) that collection of great essentials and derived materiality that the wise truly ought to see and that deserves to be seen with the eye of wisdom that penetrates ultimate reality. Loko — People blind in the eye of wisdom that penetrates ultimate reality. Paññācakkhunā — With the eye of wisdom that penetrates ultimate reality. Bhūtato — In accordance with reality. Na passati — Does not know or see.
v1-pA.V1-A-06: Apassaṃ — Not knowing or seeing things as they are with the eye of wisdom that penetrates ultimate reality. Mūḷho — One who is deluded, perceiving things wrongly. Bajjhate — Is bound by craving. Bajjhamāno — One being bound by craving. Na muccati — Cannot escape the suffering of the round of defilements or the suffering of the round of saṃsāra.2
v1-pA.V1-A-07: Someone blind in the eye of wisdom that penetrates ultimate reality fails to know things as they are with that eye. Such a person fails to recognise visible form as visible form, the collection of body parts beginning with head hair as the collection of body parts beginning with head hair, the material body (rūpakāya), the collection of instances of materiality as a collection of great essentials and derived materiality, the mental body (nāmakāya), the collection of instances of mentality as the mental body (nāmakāya), the collection of instances of mentality, the collection of causes and effects as the collection of causes and effects, the collections of impermanent, suffering, non-self and foul phenomena as collections of impermanent phenomena, of suffering phenomena, of non-self phenomena and of foul phenomena. Instead, being deluded, that person mistakenly perceives a man, a woman and so forth. For one who sees mistakenly and is thus deluded, in relation to those men, women and…

v1-pB.V1-B-01: …those other objects, craving, the attachment that clings to them, entwines and binds that person. One who is entwined and bound by craving cannot escape this saṃsāra, in which the three rounds, the round of defilements (kilesavaṭṭa), the round of kamma (kammavaṭṭa), and the round of results (vipākavaṭṭa), turn without interruption.
v1-pB.V1-B-02: A good person endowed with the knowledge of right view, the eye of wisdom that penetrates ultimate reality, sees as follows.
v1-pB.V1-B-03:
1. Visible form as visible form.
  2. The collection of body parts beginning with head hair as the collection of body parts beginning with head hair.
  3. The material body (rūpakāya), the collection of instances of materiality as a collection of great essentials and derived materiality.
  4. The mental body (nāmakāya), the collection of instances of mentality as the mental body (nāmakāya), the collection of instances of mentality.
  5. The collection of causes and effects as the collection of causes and effects.
  6. The collections of impermanent, suffering, non-self and foul phenomena as collections of impermanent phenomena, of suffering phenomena, of non-self phenomena and of foul phenomena.
v1-pB.V1-B-04: With the knowledge of right view, the eye of wisdom that penetrates ultimate reality, this person directly penetrates, knows and sees for themselves. Craving cannot bind a good person who penetrates, knows and sees in this way without delusion. Free from the entanglement and bondage of craving, such a person can escape the defilements and the suffering of the round of saṃsāra.
v1-pB.V1-B-05: This is the meaning of the verse above.
v1-pB.V1-B-06: The vision of a person blind in the eye of wisdom, whose knowledge and vision fall short of ultimate reality, differs from that of a good person endowed with the eye of wisdom, the knowledge of right view that reaches ultimate reality. A person blind in the eye of wisdom does not see as far as ultimate reality. A good person endowed with that eye sees all the way to ultimate reality.
v1-pB.V1-B-07:
Taking this verse as their basis, the good people of old said:

  1. Though one sees, one does not see.
  2. Though one hears, one does not hear.
  3. Though one smells, one does not smell.
  4. Though one relishes a taste, one does not know the taste.
  5. Though one touches, one does not know.
  6. Though one knows, one does not know.

In this way they spoke of mistaken perception with respect to all six kinds of objects.4

v1-p2.V1-2-01:
One Auspicious Night (Bhaddekaratta Sutta)

Before presenting the section on the Bhaddekaratta Sutta, I will first explain direct knowledge (paccakkhañāṇa) and inferential knowledge (anvayañāṇa). Meditators should know about these beforehand in connection with contemplating the past and the future.
v1-p2.V1-2-02:
Direct Knowledge and Inferential Knowledge

Aniccato manasikaroto adhimokkhabahulassa saddhindriyaṃ ādhipateyyaṃ hoti, bhāvanāya cattārindriyāni tadanvayā honti, …

For one who attends to things as impermanent and is strong in resolution, the faculty of faith takes the leading role. Through development, the other four faculties follow it, …19

Tadanvayā hontīti taṃ anugāminī taṃ anuvattinī honti.

“They follow it” means that they go after it and conform to it.20
v1-p2.V1-2-03:
Paññavato bhikkhave ariyasāvakassa tadanvayā saddhā saṇṭhāti, …

Bhikkhus, in a noble disciple endowed with wisdom, faith becomes established in conformity with that wisdom, …21

Tadanvayāti taṃ anugacchamānā, anuvattamānāti attho.

“In conformity with it” means going after it and following it.22
v1-p2.V1-2-04:
Anvaye ñāṇanti cattāri saccāni paccakkhato disvā yathā idāni, evaṃ atītepi anāgatepi imeva pañcakkhandhā dukkhasaccaṃ, ayameva taṇhā samudayasaccaṃ, ayameva nirodho nirodhasaccaṃ, ayameva maggo maggasaccanti evaṃ tassa ñāṇassa anugatiyaṃ ñāṇaṃ.

“Inferential knowledge”: having seen the four truths directly, one knows in the wake of that knowledge: “As now, so too in the past and in the future, these very five aggregates are the truth of suffering, this very craving is the truth of origin, this very cessation is the truth of cessation, and this very path is the truth of the path.”23

Anvaye ñāṇanti anugamanañāṇaṃ. Paccakkhato disvāti cattāri saccāni maggañāṇena paccakkhato paṭivijjhitvā.

“Inferential knowledge” means knowledge that follows. “Having seen directly” means having directly penetrated the four truths with path knowledge.24
v1-p2.V1-2-05:
According to the Pāli, commentaries and subcommentaries quoted above, there are two kinds of following: phenomena that follow something (tadanvayadhamma), and inferential knowledge. There are also two kinds of inferential knowledge:

  1. Inferential knowledge that follows insight knowledge.
  2. Inferential knowledge that follows knowledge of the noble path and fruition.

Of these two kinds of inferential knowledge, I will first present the inferential knowledge that follows insight knowledge.
v1-p2.V1-2-06:
Excerpt from the Upanisā Sutta

Jānato ahaṃ bhikkhave passato āsavānaṃ khayaṃ vadāmi, no ajānato no apassato. Kiñca bhikkhave jānato kiṃ passato āsavānaṃ khayo hoti?

Bhikkhus, I speak of the destruction of the taints for one who knows and sees, not for one who does not know and does not see. Bhikkhus, for one who knows and sees what is there destruction of the taints?

  1. Iti rūpaṃ, iti rūpassa samudayo, iti rūpassa atthaṅgamo. — Such is materiality, such is its arising, and such is its disappearance.
  2. Iti vedanā. (as above) — Such is feeling. (as above)
  3. Iti saññā. — Such is perception.
  4. Iti saṅkhārā. — Such are formations.
  5. Iti viññāṇaṃ, iti viññāṇassa samudayo, iti viññāṇassa atthaṅgamoti. — Such is consciousness, such is its arising, and such is its disappearance.25

v1-p3.V1-3-01: Bhikkhus, I declare the noble path and fruition that bring the taints to an end for one who personally penetrates and knows with the knowledge of right view, and personally penetrates and sees with the knowledge of right view. I do not declare the noble path and fruition that bring the taints to an end for one who neither personally penetrates and knows nor personally penetrates and sees with the knowledge of right view.
v1-p3.V1-3-02: Bhikkhus, when someone personally penetrates and knows what with the knowledge of right view, and personally penetrates and sees what with the knowledge of right view, do the noble path and fruition that bring the taints to an end arise?
v1-p3.V1-3-03:
1. (a) This is materiality. (b) This is the cause of the arising of materiality, and this is its arising. (c) This is the cause of the cessation of materiality, and this is its cessation.
  2. (a) This is feeling. (b) This is the cause of the arising of feeling, and this is its arising. (c) This is the cause of the cessation of feeling, and this is its cessation.
  3. (a) This is perception. (b) This is the cause of the arising of perception, and this is its arising. (c) This is the cause of the cessation of perception, and this is its cessation.
  4. (a) These are formations, the mental factors. (b) This is the cause of their arising, and this is their arising. (c) This is the cause of their cessation, and this is their cessation.
  5. (a) This is consciousness. (b) This is the cause of the arising of consciousness, and this is its arising. (c) This is the cause of the cessation of consciousness, and this is its cessation.
v1-p3.V1-3-04: For one who personally penetrates and knows with the knowledge of right view, and personally penetrates and sees with the knowledge of right view in this way, the noble path and fruition that bring the taints to an end arise.25
v1-p3.V1-3-05:
The meaning of this teaching is as follows.

  1. The five aggregates.
  2. Their cause of arising (samudaya) and their actual arising (samudaya = udaya).
  3. Their cause of cessation (atthaṅgama) and their actual disappearance (atthaṅgama = vaya).

Only for one who personally penetrates and knows with the knowledge of right view, and personally penetrates and sees with the knowledge of right view these things can the knowledge of the noble path and fruition that brings the taints to an end arise. If, with the knowledge of right view…

v1-p4.V1-4-01: …one does not personally penetrate and know, or personally penetrate and see, the knowledge of the noble path and fruition that brings the taints to an end cannot arise. This is the intended meaning.
v1-p4.V1-4-02: The commentary and subcommentary also explain the meaning of that passage as follows.
v1-p4.V1-4-03:
Jānatoti jānantassa. Passatoti passantassa. Dvepi padāni ekatthāni, byañjanameva nānaṃ. Evaṃ santepi “jānato”ti ñāṇalakkhaṇaṃ upādāya puggalaṃ niddisati. Jānanalakkhaṇaṃ hi ñāṇaṃ. “Passato”ti ñāṇappabhāvaṃ upādāya. Passanappabhāvaṃ hi ñāṇaṃ. Ñāṇasamaṅgīpuggalo cakkhumā viya cakkhunā rūpāni, ñāṇena vivaṭe dhamme passati. (as above)

“For one who knows” means for one who is knowing. “For one who sees” means for one who is seeing. The two expressions have the same meaning. Only the wording differs. Even so, “for one who knows” designates the person with reference to the characteristic of knowledge, for the characteristic of knowledge is knowing. “For one who sees” refers to the power of knowledge, for the power of knowledge is seeing. A person endowed with knowledge sees with knowledge the phenomena it has disclosed, just as a person with eyes sees visible forms with the eye. (as above)
v1-p4.V1-4-04:
No ajānato no apassatoti yo pana na jānāti na passati, tassa no vadāmīti attho. Etena ye ajānato apassatopi saṃsārādīhiyeva suddhiṃ vadanti, te paṭikkhittā honti. Purimena padadvayena upāyo vutto, iminā anupāyaṃ paṭisedheti.

“Not for one who does not know and does not see” means that I do not make this declaration for someone who neither knows nor sees. This refutes those who maintain that even without knowing or seeing one becomes purified merely by going through saṃsāra and the like. The preceding pair of expressions sets out the means. This pair rules out what is no means.26
v1-p4.V1-4-05:
1. Jānato passatoti ettha dassanaṃ paññācakkhunāva dassanaṃ adhippetaṃ, na maṃsacakkhunāti āha “dvepi padāni ekatthānī”ti. Evaṃ santepīti padadvayassa ekatthattepi ñāṇalakkhaṇañāṇappabhāvavisayassa tathādassanabhāvāvirodhanāti attho. Tenāha “jānanalakkhaṇaṃ hi ñāṇa”ntiādi. Ñāṇappabhāvanti ñāṇānubhāvena ñāṇakiccavisayobhāsanti attho. Tenāha “ñāṇena vivaṭe dhamme passatī”ti. Jānato passatoti ca jānanadassanamukhena puggalādhiṭṭhānā desanā pavattāti āha “ñāṇalakkhaṇaṃ upādāyā”tiādi.

In “for one who knows and sees”, seeing with the eye of wisdom is intended, as distinct from seeing with the physical eye. Hence the statement that both expressions have the same meaning. “Even so” means that the two expressions having one meaning is compatible with presenting the characteristic and power of knowledge as described. Hence “the characteristic of knowledge is knowing”, and so on. “The power of knowledge” means that through the efficacy of knowledge the object is illuminated, which is the function of knowledge. Hence “one sees with knowledge the phenomena it has disclosed”. “For one who knows and sees” presents the teaching in terms of a person by way of knowing and seeing. Hence “with reference to the characteristic of knowledge”, and so on.27
v1-p4.V1-4-06:
Ñāṇalakkhaṇanti ñāṇassa sabhāvaṃ, visayassa yathāsabhāvāvabodhananti attho.

“The characteristic of knowledge” means its nature, the understanding of the object in accordance with its actual nature.28

Ñāṇappabhāvanti ñāṇānubhāvaṃ, ñāṇakiccaṃ visayobhāsananti attho.

“The power of knowledge” means its efficacy, the illumination of the object that is the function of knowledge.29
v1-p4.V1-4-07:
2. Jānatoti vā pubbabhāgañāṇena jānato, aparabhāgena ñāṇena passato.

Or “for one who knows” refers to someone who knows by the knowledge of an earlier stage, and “for one who sees” to someone who sees by the knowledge of a later stage.27
v1-p4.V1-4-08:
3. Jānatoti vā vatvā na jānanaṃ anussavākāraparivitakkamattavasena idhādhippetaṃ, atha kho rūpāni viya cakkhuviññāṇena rūpādīni tesaṃ ca samudayādike paccakkhe katvā dassananti vibhāvetuṃ “passato”ti vuttanti evaṃ vā ettha attho.

Or, having said “for one who knows”, the text adds “for one who sees” to make clear that the knowing intended here goes beyond mere oral tradition or reasoned reflection. It is seeing by bringing materiality and the remaining phenomena, together with their arising and so forth, directly before oneself, as when visible forms are seen by eye-consciousness. This is another interpretation.27
v1-p4.V1-4-09:
Jānato eva passato evāti evamettha niyamo icchito, na aññathā visesābhāvato aniṭṭhāpannovāti tassa niyamassa phalaṃ dassetuṃ “no ajānato no apassato”ti vuttanti āha “yo pana na jānāti, na passati, tassa no vadāmīti attho”ti. Iminā khandhānaṃ pariññā āsavakkhayassa ekantikakāraṇanti dasseti.

The restriction intended here is “only for one who knows, only for one who sees”. Otherwise there would be no distinction and an unwelcome consequence would follow. To show the consequence of this restriction, the text says “not for one who does not know and does not see”. Hence the explanation, “I do not make this declaration for someone who neither knows nor sees.” This shows that full understanding of the aggregates is an indispensable condition for the destruction of the taints.30
v1-p4.V1-4-10:
Paccakkhakaraṇatthena ñātapariññā tīraṇapariññā ca gahitā hoti.

The sense of bringing things directly before oneself includes both full understanding as knowing (ñātapariññā) and full understanding as investigation (tīraṇapariññā).31
v1-p4.V1-4-11:
The main point of these explanations in the commentary and subcommentary is as follows.

Jānato (“for one who knows”) and passato (“for one who sees”) have the same meaning. Only the wording differs. Even though the wording differs and the meaning is the same…

v1-p5.V1-5-01: …the expression jānato designates someone capable of knowing by reference to the characteristic of penetrating the true nature of the object as it really is. For knowledge, that is, the knowledge of right view, has the characteristic of penetrating and knowing the true nature of the object as it really is.
v1-p5.V1-5-02: The expression passato designates someone capable of seeing by reference to the power and efficacy of knowledge to see the true nature of the object. For knowledge, that is, the knowledge of right view, has the power and efficacy to see the true nature of the object. A person with the sensitive matter of the eye (pasādacakkhu) sees visible forms by means of it, that is, by eye-consciousness. Likewise, someone endowed with the knowledge of right view sees the phenomena disclosed by knowledge, whose function is to illuminate the object so that its true nature can be seen.32
v1-p5.V1-5-03: No ajānato no apassato means “not for one who does not know and does not see”. The meaning is that I do not declare the noble path and fruition that bring the taints to an end for someone who neither knows nor sees the five aggregates subject to clinging, their arising or their disappearance. This expression refutes those who hold that one can be purified merely by going through saṃsāra and the like without knowing or seeing the five aggregates subject to clinging, their arising or their disappearance.32
v1-p5.V1-5-04: The first pair of expressions, jānato passato, teaches the way to bring the taints to an end. The pair no ajānato no apassato rules out what is no way to bring the taints to an end.32
v1-p5.V1-5-05: The venerable author of the subcommentary then explains the meaning of the commentary in three ways, as follows.
v1-p5.V1-5-06: 1. In the expressions jānato passato, “for one who knows and sees”, seeing means seeing with the eye of wisdom (paññācakkhu). It does not mean seeing with the physical eye (maṃsacakkhu), the ordinary eye with its sensitive matter. This is why the commentator explains that jānato and passato have the same meaning.
v1-p5.V1-5-07:
Evaṃ santepi (“even so”) indicates that, although the expressions jānato and passato have the same meaning, there is:

  1. The object of the characteristic of knowledge (ñāṇalakkhaṇa), which is penetrating and knowing the actual nature of the object as it is.
  2. The object of the power of knowledge (ñāṇappabhāva), which is to illuminate the object so that its actual nature can be penetrated and seen.

v1-p6.V1-6-01: With respect to this object, the two expressions are compatible in the sense of knowing and seeing just explained. This is why the commentator says Jānanalakkhaṇaṃ hi ñāṇaṃ, “Knowledge has the characteristic of knowing”, that is, of penetrating and knowing the actual nature of its object as it is.
v1-p6.V1-6-02:
The power of knowledge (ñāṇappabhāva) is its efficacy. From this efficacy comes the light of knowledge, whose function is to illuminate the object so that its actual nature can be seen as it is. This agrees with the Aṭṭhasālinī: Visayobhāsarasā padīpo viya, “Its function is to illuminate the object, like a lamp.”33 The commentator accordingly says Ñāṇena vivaṭe dhamme passati, “One sees with knowledge the phenomena it has disclosed.” A person who sees with the knowledge of right view sees phenomena disclosed by the knowledge whose function is to illuminate their true nature.34

Author’s note. For the light of knowledge, see pp. 510–534 of this work.
v1-p6.V1-6-03: 1. Alternatively, jānato refers to one who knows by the knowledge that arises earlier, and passato to one who sees by the knowledge that arises later.
v1-p6.V1-6-04:
1. Alternatively, having said “for one who knows” (jānato), the Buddha goes on to say “for one who sees” (passato). The knowing intended here is more than the following two kinds.
  1. Oral tradition (anussava), knowing from what one has learned by hearing it from teachers, parents and others.
  2. Reasoned reflection (ākāraparivitakka), knowing by considering and weighing suitable reasons.

Instead, just as visible forms are seen by eye-consciousness, one personally knows and sees by direct knowledge (paccakkhañāṇa):

  1. The five aggregates subject to clinging: materiality, feeling, perception, formations and consciousness.
  2. The cause of the arising of these five aggregates (samudaya), and their actual arising (samudaya in the sense of udaya).
  3. The cause of their cessation (atthaṅgama), and their actual disappearance (atthaṅgama in the sense of vaya).

It is to make this meaning clear that the Buddha says “for one who sees”. The meaning here should also be understood in this way.34
v1-p6.V1-6-05:
Oral Tradition and Reasoned Reflection

Here I will explain oral tradition (anussava) and reasoned reflection (ākāraparivitakka) in a little more detail.
v1-p6.V1-6-06:
Anu anu savanaṃ anussavo.

Hearing successively, one after another, is oral tradition.35
v1-p6.V1-6-07:
Paramparāgatassa atthassa evaṃ kirassāti anussavanaṃ.

Hearing of a meaning handed down through successive generations as “It is said to be so.”36

v1-p7.V1-7-01: Knowing, that is, learned knowledge acquired by hearing from parents, grandparents, teachers and others through successive generations, is called oral tradition (anussava). Knowledge of the five aggregates subject to clinging and of their arising and disappearance acquired merely by hearing from parents, grandparents, teachers and others is not the knowing intended by “for one who knows” (jānato) and “for one who sees” (passato) in this Upanisā Sutta. Such learned knowledge is not here called the knowing that brings the taints to an end.
v1-p7.V1-7-02:
Ākāraparivitakkoti yuttiparikappanā.

“Reasoned reflection” is the formulation of ideas on the basis of reasoning.36
v1-p7.V1-7-03: Thinking over, weighing and considering suitable reasons is called reasoned reflection (ākāraparivitakka). Knowing merely through such reflection is also not what “for one who knows” and “for one who sees” mean in this Upanisā Sutta. The Buddha’s Dhamma is beyond the sphere of reasoning (atakkāvacara): it does not lie within reach of reasoners who merely think and imagine without practising.37
v1-p7.V1-7-04:
Direct Knowledge

Katamā ca bhikkhave sammādiṭṭhi? Yaṃ kho bhikkhave dukkhe ñāṇaṃ, dukkhasamudaye ñāṇaṃ, dukkhanirodhe ñāṇaṃ, dukkhanirodhagāminiyā paṭipadāya ñāṇaṃ. Ayaṃ vuccati bhikkhave sammādiṭṭhi.

And what, bhikkhus, is right view? Knowledge of suffering, knowledge of the origin of suffering, knowledge of the cessation of suffering, and knowledge of the practice leading to the cessation of suffering: this, bhikkhus, is called right view.38
v1-p7.V1-7-05:
Bhikkhus, what is right view (sammādiṭṭhi)? Bhikkhus:

  1. Knowledge of the truth of suffering (dukkhasacca).
  2. Knowledge of the truth of origin (samudayasacca), the cause of suffering.
  3. Knowledge of the truth of cessation (nirodhasacca), which brings suffering to an end.
  4. Knowledge of the truth of the path (maggasacca), the practice leading to Nibbāna, where suffering ceases.

Such knowledge, bhikkhus, is called right view.38
v1-p7.V1-7-06: In accordance with these teachings, the four kinds of knowledge of right view, called right view of the four truths (catusaccasammādiṭṭhi), are called direct knowledge (paccakkhañāṇa). Only someone who personally penetrates, knows and sees with that direct knowledge is called “one who knows” and “one who sees” in this discourse.
v1-p7.V1-7-07:
1. The five aggregates subject to clinging.
  2. Their actual arising.
  3. Their actual disappearance.

Only for one who knows and sees these with that direct knowledge does the teaching say that the noble path and fruition bringing the taints to an end can be attained. As for someone who, by that direct knowledge, does not know or see these three kinds of phenomena…

v1-p8.V1-8-01: …the Buddha does not teach that such a person can attain the noble path and fruition that bring the taints to an end.
v1-p8.V1-8-02:
All good people seeking the noble path and fruition that bring the taints to an end should therefore understand that they must first strive to penetrate, know and see personally, with direct knowledge, the knowledge of right view described above:

  1. The five aggregates subject to clinging.
  2. The actual arising of those five aggregates.
  3. The actual disappearance of those five aggregates.

Contemplation by inferential knowledge (anvayañāṇa) will be explained later.
v1-p8.V1-8-03: I will now explain the aggregates subject to clinging, their actual arising and their actual disappearance individually.
v1-p8.V1-8-04:
What Is an Aggregate Subject to Clinging?

Yaṃ kiñci bhikkhave rūpaṃ atītānāgatapaccuppannaṃ ajjhattaṃ vā bahiddhā vā oḷārikaṃ vā sukhumaṃ vā hīnaṃ vā paṇītaṃ vā yaṃ dūre santike vā sāsavaṃ upādāniyaṃ, ayaṃ vuccati rūpupādānakkhandho.

Bhikkhus, whatever materiality there is, past, future or present, internal or external, gross or subtle, inferior or superior, far or near, that is subject to the taints and liable to be clung to, is called the materiality aggregate subject to clinging.39
v1-p8.V1-8-05:
That is, all materiality in the following eleven categories, which exists in the thirty-one planes, is an object of the taints, and is taken hold of by craving and views as “I” and “mine”:

  1. All past materiality (atīta).
  2. All future materiality (anāgata).
  3. All present materiality (paccuppanna).
  4. All internal materiality (ajjhatta).
  5. All external materiality (bahiddhā).
  6. All gross materiality (oḷārika).
  7. All subtle materiality (sukhuma).
  8. All inferior materiality (hīna).
  9. All superior materiality (paṇīta).
  10. All distant materiality (dūra), distant from the knowledge of the meditator contemplating it.
  11. All near materiality (santika), near to the knowledge of the meditator contemplating it.

All materiality existing in these eleven categories is called the materiality aggregate subject to clinging (rūpupādānakkhandha).39

v1-p9.V1-9-01:
Similarly, the teaching goes on to explain each of the remaining aggregates separately.

All feeling existing in these eleven categories is called the feeling aggregate subject to clinging (vedanupādānakkhandha).

All perception existing in these eleven categories is called the perception aggregate subject to clinging (saññupādānakkhandha).

All mental factors belonging to formations existing in these eleven categories are called the formations aggregate subject to clinging (saṅkhārupādānakkhandha).

All instances of consciousness existing in these eleven categories are called the consciousness aggregate subject to clinging (viññāṇupādānakkhandha).39
v1-p9.V1-9-02:
Therefore, with reference to the five aggregates subject to clinging that exist in these eleven categories, are objects of the taints, and are taken hold of by craving and views as “I” and “mine”, the Buddha teaches in the Upanisā Sutta quoted above:

  1. Iti rūpaṃ — This is materiality.
  2. Iti vedanā — This is feeling.
  3. Iti saññā — This is perception.
  4. Iti saṅkhārā — These are the mental factors belonging to formations.
  5. Iti viññāṇaṃ — This is consciousness.
v1-p9.V1-9-03: In teaching this, what kind of knowing does the Buddha intend by “This is materiality; this is feeling; this is perception; these are the mental factors belonging to formations; this is consciousness”? The answer is as follows.
v1-p9.V1-9-04:
“This Is Materiality”, “This Is Feeling”…

Tattha iti rūpanti idaṃ rūpaṃ, ettakaṃ rūpaṃ, ito uddhaṃ rūpaṃ natthīti ruppanasabhāvañceva bhūtupādāyabhedañca ādiṃ katvā lakkhaṇa-rasa-paccupaṭṭhāna-padaṭṭhānavasena anavasesarūpapariggaho vutto. (as above)

Here, “this is materiality” means: “This is materiality. This is the full extent of materiality. Beyond this there is no materiality.” This states the complete discernment of materiality, without remainder, by characteristic, function, manifestation and proximate cause, beginning with its nature of being affected by change and its division into great essentials and derived materiality. (as above)40
v1-p9.V1-9-05:
Iti vedanātiādīsupi ayaṃ vedanā, ettakā vedanā, ito uddhaṃ vedanā natthi; ayaṃ saññā. Ime saṅkhārā. Idaṃ viññāṇaṃ, ettakaṃ viññāṇaṃ, ito uddhaṃ viññāṇaṃ natthīti vedayita-sañjānana-abhisaṅkhāraṇa-vijānanasabhāvañceva sukhādi-rūpasaññādi-phassādi-cakkhuviññāṇādibhedañca ādiṃ katvā lakkhaṇa-rasa-paccupaṭṭhāna-padaṭṭhānavasena anavasesa-vedanā-saññā-saṅkhāra-viññāṇapariggaho vutto.

The same applies to “this is feeling” and the rest: “This is feeling. This is the full extent of feeling. Beyond this there is no feeling. This is perception. These are formations. This is consciousness. This is the full extent of consciousness. Beyond this there is no consciousness.” This states the complete discernment of feeling, perception, formations and consciousness, without remainder, by characteristic, function, manifestation and proximate cause. It begins with their respective natures of feeling, perceiving, constructing and cognising, and their divisions into happiness and the rest, perception of visible form and the rest, contact and the rest, and eye-consciousness and the rest.40
v1-p9.V1-9-06:
Iti rūpanti ettha iti-saddo idaṃ-saddena samānatthoti adhippāyenāha “idaṃ rūpa”nti. Tayidaṃ sarūpaggahaṇabhāvato anavasesapariyādānaṃ hotīti āha “ettakaṃ rūpaṃ, na ito paraṃ rūpaṃ

In “this is materiality”, the word iti is understood to have the same meaning as idaṃ, hence the explanation “this is materiality”. Since this is a grasping of its actual nature that embraces the whole without remainder, the text says: “This is the full extent of materiality. Beyond this no materiality…

v1-p10.V1-10-01:
atthī”ti. Itīti vā pakāratthe nipāto, tasmā “iti rūpa”nti iminā bhūtupādādivasena yattako rūpassa pabhedo, tena saddhiṃ rūpaṃ anavasesato pariyādiyitvā dasseti. Sabhāvatoti ruppanasabhāvato, cakkhādi-vaṇṇādisabhāvato ca. Vedanādīsupīti ettha “ayaṃ vedanā, ettakā vedanā, na ito paraṃ vedanā atthīti sabhāvato vedanaṃ pajānātī”ti ādinā, sabhāvatoti ca “anubhavanasabhāvato, sātādisabhāvato cā”ti evamādinā yojetabbaṃ.

…exists.” Alternatively, iti is an indeclinable indicating manner. Thus “this is materiality” presents all materiality exhaustively, together with its full division into great essentials, derived materiality and so forth. “According to its nature” means its nature of being affected by change, and the natures of the eye and the rest, of colour and the rest. “The same applies to feeling and the rest” is to be construed as: “This is feeling. This is the full extent of feeling. Beyond this no feeling exists: one understands feeling according to its nature.” “According to its nature” is to be construed as “according to its nature of experiencing, and its nature of being pleasant and so forth”, and similarly for the remaining aggregates.41
v1-p10.V1-10-02: Question. The Buddha instructs the meditator bhikkhu to dwell continually contemplating and developing the knowledge of right view with regard to the five aggregates subject to clinging: “This is materiality. This is feeling. This is perception. These are the mental factors belonging to formations. This is consciousness.” When instructed in this way, how should the meditator bhikkhu know these five aggregates? How should he contemplate them with the knowledge of right view?
v1-p10.V1-10-03:
Answer. The answer is as follows.

  1. “This is materiality. This is the full extent of materiality. There is nothing further beyond this.” The meaning is to discern and distinguish all materiality without remainder with the knowledge of right view, according to characteristic, function, manifestation and proximate cause, beginning with its nature of being affected by change (ruppanasabhāva) and the twenty-eight kinds of materiality, comprising great essentials and derived materiality. Being affected by change means that, owing to causes such as cold and heat, a later material process arises in various changed forms differing from the process that arose before. This is a common characteristic (sāmaññalakkhaṇa) that pertains to all materiality. In other words, one must know, must contemplate so as to know, all materiality without remainder, with the knowledge of right view according to characteristic, function, manifestation and proximate cause.
v1-p10.V1-10-04:
The same applies to “this is feeling” and the rest.

  1. This is feeling. This is the full extent of feeling. Beyond this there is no further feeling.
  2. This is perception. (as above)
  3. These are the mental factors belonging to formations. (as above)
  4. This is consciousness. This is the full extent of consciousness. Beyond this there is no further consciousness.
v1-p10.V1-10-05:
1. The nature of the feeling aggregate (vedanākkhandha) is to experience the flavour of the object.
  2. The nature of the perception aggregate (saññākkhandha) is to recognise by taking a sign of the object.
  3. The nature of the formations aggregate (saṅkhārakkhandha) is to construct and bring about the resultant phenomenon that its causes jointly accomplish, causing it to arise.
  4. The nature of the consciousness aggregate (viññāṇakkhandha) is to distinguish and take up the object, to cognise it.
v1-p10.V1-10-06:
1. The division of the feeling aggregate into happiness and the rest.
  2. The division of the perception aggregate into perception of visible form and the rest.

v1-p11.V1-11-01:
1. The division of the formations aggregate into contact (phassa), volition (cetanā), and the rest.
  2. The division of the consciousness aggregate into eye-consciousness and the rest.

Beginning with these, the teaching means that feeling, perception, formations and consciousness are to be discerned and distinguished completely, without remainder, by characteristic, function, manifestation and proximate cause. In other words, one must know, must contemplate so as to know, all instances of feeling, perception, formations and consciousness completely, without remainder, with the knowledge of right view by characteristic, function, manifestation and proximate cause.43
v1-p11.V1-11-02:
In accordance with the explanations of the commentary and subcommentary above, the meditator must personally discern and contemplate the following completely, without remainder, so as directly to penetrate, know and see them with the knowledge of right view:

  1. The twenty-eight kinds of materiality comprising great essentials and derived materiality, and the respective characteristic, function, manifestation and proximate cause of each, such as the earth element (pathavī), water element (āpo), fire element (tejo) and wind element (vāyo).
  2. The kinds of feeling: bodily pleasant feeling (sukhavedanā), bodily painful feeling (dukkhavedanā), mentally pleasant feeling (somanassavedanā), mentally painful feeling (domanassavedanā), and equanimous feeling (upekkhāvedanā), with the characteristic, function, manifestation and proximate cause of each.
  3. The kinds of perception: perception of visible form (rūpasaññā), sound (saddasaññā), odour (gandhasaññā), flavour (rasasaññā), tangible objects (phoṭṭhabbasaññā) and mental objects (dhammasaññā), with the characteristic, function, manifestation and proximate cause of each.
  4. The kinds of formations, the fifty mental factors belonging to the formations aggregate, including contact (phassa), volition (cetanā), one-pointedness (ekaggatā), life faculty (jīvita), attention (manasikāra), and the rest, with the characteristic, function, manifestation and proximate cause of each mental factor.
  5. The kinds of consciousness: eye-consciousness (cakkhuviññāṇa), ear-consciousness (sotaviññāṇa), nose-consciousness (ghānaviññāṇa), tongue-consciousness (jivhāviññāṇa), body-consciousness (kāyaviññāṇa) and mind-consciousness (manoviññāṇa), with the characteristic, function, manifestation and proximate cause of each.
v1-p11.V1-11-03:
Only knowing and seeing in this way is called knowing and seeing:

  1. This is materiality.
  2. This is feeling.
  3. This is perception.
  4. These are formations.
  5. This is consciousness.

When contemplating so as to know and see in this way:
v1-p11.V1-11-04:
Cakkhumā viya cakkhunā rūpāni.

“Like a person with eyes seeing visible forms with the eye.”44

Rūpāni viya cakkhuviññāṇena rūpādīni tesaṃ ca samudayādike paccakkhe katvā dassanaṃ.

“Seeing by bringing materiality and the rest, together with their arising and so forth, directly before oneself, as visible forms are seen by eye-consciousness.”45
v1-p11.V1-11-05: In accordance with these explanations of the commentary and subcommentary, just as someone with eyes sees visible forms by eye-consciousness, the meditator must discern and contemplate these phenomena with the aid of the light arising from the knowledge discerning and contemplating them. One must personally penetrate, know and see them with the knowledge of right view…

v1-p12.V1-12-01:
…that is, direct knowledge (paccakkhañāṇa).

Only when knowing and seeing in this way, only for a person who knows and sees in this way, does the Buddha teach that the noble path and fruition bringing the taints to an end can be attained. He does not teach that someone who does not know or see in this way can attain the noble path and fruition bringing the taints to an end.
v1-p12.V1-12-02:
Respectfully bearing these teachings upon my head, I have set out the following in this work, Nibbānagāminipaṭipadā:

  1. The instructions for using direct knowledge, the knowledge of right view, to discern and contemplate the twenty-eight kinds of materiality in the materiality aggregate subject to clinging, one of the five aggregates subject to clinging, until knowledge penetrates ultimate reality, are set out under Materiality Meditation (Rūpakammaṭṭhāna). See Volume I.
  2. The instructions for using direct knowledge, the knowledge of right view, to discern and contemplate consciousness and mental factors belonging to the feeling, perception, formations and consciousness aggregates subject to clinging, until knowledge penetrates ultimate reality, are set out under Mentality Meditation (Nāmakammaṭṭhāna). See Volume II.
  3. The instructions for dividing and analysing the individual ultimate natures of the material and mental phenomena belonging to the five aggregates subject to clinging, and using direct knowledge, the knowledge of right view, to discern and contemplate them by characteristic, function, manifestation and proximate cause, are set out under The Four Aspects Beginning with Characteristic (Lakkhaṇādicatukka). See Volume IV.
v1-p12.V1-12-03: I will now explain the meaning of the second teaching in the Upanisā Sutta quoted above: Iti rūpassa samudayo. (as above) Iti viññāṇassa samudayo — “Such is the arising of materiality. (as above) Such is the arising of consciousness.”
v1-p12.V1-12-04:
“Such Is the Arising of Materiality” (as above) “Such Is the Arising of Consciousness”…

Iti rūpassa samudayoti evaṃ avijjāsamudayādivasena pañcahākārehi rūpassa samudayo.

“Such is the arising of materiality”: the arising of materiality is thus shown in five ways, beginning with the arising of ignorance.47
v1-p12.V1-12-05:
Tassa vitthāro “avijjāsamudayā rūpasamudayo, taṇhāsamudayā rūpasamudayo, kammasamudayā rūpasamudayo, āhārasamudayā rūpasamudayoti, nibbattilakkhaṇaṃ passantopi rūpakkhandhassa udayaṃ passatī”ti evaṃ veditabbo.

Its detailed explanation should be understood thus: “With the arising of ignorance, materiality arises. With the arising of craving, materiality arises. With the arising of kamma, materiality arises. With the arising of nutriment, materiality arises. Also, in seeing the characteristic of origination, one sees the arising of the materiality aggregate.”48
v1-p12.V1-12-06:
Avijjāsamudayāti avijjāya uppādā, atthibhāvāti attho. Nirodhanirodhī hi uppādo atthibhāvavācakopi hoti, tasmā purimabhavasiddhāya avijjāya sati imasmiṃ bhave rūpasamudayo, rūpassa uppādo hotīti attho. “Taṇhāsamudayā”tiādīsupi eseva nayo. Āhārasamudayāti ettha pana pavattipaccayesu kabaḷīkārāhārassa balavatāya so eva gahito. Tasmiṃ pana gahite pavattipaccayatāsāmaññena utucittāni gahitāneva hontīti catusamuṭṭhānikarūpassa paccayato udaya-

“With the arising of ignorance” means through the origination, the existence, of ignorance. For origination, opposed to cessation, can also denote existence. Thus the meaning is that, when ignorance established in the preceding existence is present, materiality arises in this existence. The same method applies to “with the arising of craving” and the rest. In “with the arising of nutriment”, physical nutriment alone is mentioned because of its strength among the conditions during the course of life. When it is mentioned, however, temperature and consciousness are also included, because they too are conditions during the course of life. Thus seeing the arising by way of conditions of materiality originating from four sources…49

v1-p13.V1-13-01:
dassanaṃ vibhāvitamevāti daṭṭhabbaṃ. “Nibbattilakkhaṇa”ntiādinā kālavasena udayadassanamāha. Tattha nibbattilakkhaṇanti rūpassa uppādasaṅkhātaṃ saṅkhatalakkhaṇaṃ. Passantopīti na kevalaṃ paccayasamudayameva, atha kho khaṇato udayaṃ passantopi. Addhānavasena hi paṭhamaṃ udayaṃ passitvā ṭhito puna santativasena disvā anukkamena khaṇavasena passati.

…should be understood to have been explained. “The characteristic of origination” and the rest express seeing arising in terms of time. Here “the characteristic of origination” is the characteristic of the conditioned called the origination of materiality. “Also seeing” means seeing the arising by moment in addition to seeing the arising by way of conditions. For, having first seen arising in terms of a period (addhāna), one subsequently sees it in terms of continuity (santati), and gradually in terms of a moment (khaṇa).49
v1-p13.V1-13-02:
Nibbattilakkhaṇanti addhā-santati-khaṇavasena rūpassa uppādaṃ, uppādoyeva saṅkhatalakkhaṇattā lakkhaṇanti ca vutto.

“The characteristic of origination” is the origination of materiality in terms of period, continuity and moment. Origination itself is also called a characteristic because it is a characteristic of the conditioned.50
v1-p13.V1-13-03: In accordance with the explanations of the commentary and subcommentary, which cite the Paṭisambhidāmagga, the following are to be contemplated under the teaching “such is the arising of materiality” and the rest.
v1-p13.V1-13-04:
Contemplating the Arising of the Materiality Aggregate

  1. With the arising of ignorance (avijjā), kamma-born materiality (kammaja) arises.
  2. With the arising of craving (taṇhā), kamma-born materiality arises.
  3. With the arising of clinging (upādāna), kamma-born materiality arises.
  4. With the arising of formations (saṅkhāra), kamma-born materiality arises.
  5. With the arising of kamma, kamma-born materiality arises.

• The actual arising of kamma-born materiality.

  1. With the arising of consciousness (citta), consciousness-born materiality (cittaja) arises.

• The actual arising of consciousness-born materiality.

  1. With the arising of temperature (utu), temperature-born materiality (utuja) arises.

• The actual arising of temperature-born materiality.

  1. With the arising of nutriment (āhāra), nutriment-born materiality (āhāraja) arises.

• The actual arising of nutriment-born materiality.
v1-p13.V1-13-05: These are the matters to be contemplated. For the detailed method, see Volume V, the Insight Section — Detailed Contemplation of Arising and Passing Away — Contemplating the Nature of Arising (Samudayadhammānupassī).
v1-p13.V1-13-06:
Among these, contemplating so as to know and see how an effect arises because its cause has arisen or existed, as in “with the arising of ignorance, kamma-born materiality arises”, is called seeing arising by way of conditions (paccayato udayadassana). It is contemplating the actual arising in terms of its causes.

Contemplating so as to know and see the actual arising of each group of effects corresponding to its causes, such as the arising of kamma-born materiality and of consciousness-born materiality, is called seeing arising by moment (khaṇato udayadassana). It is contemplating arising in terms of moments. When contemplating these matters too:

v1-p14.V1-14-01:
Cakkhumā viya cakkhunā rūpāni…

“Like a person with eyes seeing visible forms with the eye…”44

Rūpāni viya cakkhuviññāṇena rūpādīni tesaṃ ca samudayādike paccakkhe katvā dassanaṃ…

“Seeing by bringing materiality and the rest, together with their arising and so forth, directly before oneself, as visible forms are seen by eye-consciousness…”45
v1-p14.V1-14-02: In accordance with these explanations of the commentary and subcommentary, just as someone with eyes sees visible forms by eye-consciousness, the meditator must discern and contemplate these phenomena with the aid of the light arising from the knowledge discerning and contemplating them. One must personally penetrate, know and see them with direct knowledge, the knowledge of right view.
v1-p14.V1-14-03:
To contemplate in this way, the meditator must already have discerned:

  1. The respective causes, such as ignorance, craving, clinging, formations and kamma.
  2. The respective effects, materiality, feeling, perception, formations and consciousness.
  3. Their causal relationship: the arising of each respective effect through its respective cause.

This is the domain of knowledge of delimitation of mentality and materiality (nāmarūpaparicchedañāṇa) and knowledge of discernment of conditions (paccayapariggahañāṇa).
v1-p14.V1-14-04: Only a meditator who has reached the far shore of knowledge of delimitation of mentality and materiality and knowledge of discernment of conditions can contemplate in this way under “contemplating the nature of arising” (samudayadhammānupassī). The author of the Visuddhimagga accordingly includes this contemplation in the section on knowledge of arising and passing away (udayabbayañāṇa). See Visuddhimagga, vol. II, p. 266.51
v1-p14.V1-14-05: In this contemplation, when did ignorance, craving, clinging, formations and kamma arise? They are the fundamental causes of the material and mental phenomena in the present five aggregates subject to clinging that belong to the round of results (vipākavaṭṭa). To find the answer, read the following extract from the Paṭisambhidāmagga.
v1-p14.V1-14-06:
Excerpt from the Paṭisambhidāmagga

Five Past Causes

Purimakammabhavasmiṃ moho avijjā, āyūhanā saṅkhārā, nikanti taṇhā, upagamanaṃ upādānaṃ, cetanā bhavoti ime pañca dhammā purimakammabhavasmiṃ idha paṭisandhiyā paccayā.

“In the previous kamma-existence, delusion is ignorance, accumulation is formations, attachment is craving, approaching is clinging, and volition is existence. These five phenomena in the previous kamma-existence are conditions for rebirth-linking here.”52
v1-p14.V1-14-07:
Tattha purimakammabhavasminti purime kammabhave, atītajātiyaṃ kammabhave kariyamāneti attho.

Here “in the previous kamma-existence” means in the former kamma-existence, when kamma-existence was being produced in the past birth.53

v1-p15.V1-15-01:
When producing and accumulating the kamma called kamma-existence (kammabhava) in the past life:

  1. Not knowing the four truths and wrongly perceiving a man, a woman, a person, a being, a human, a deity, a brahmā and so forth is ignorance (avijjā).
  2. The wholesome and unwholesome phenomena that produce the five aggregates, such as human existence with its human aggregates and deva existence with its deva aggregates, are formations (saṅkhārā).
  3. Attachment to and desire for those existences and sense objects, such as human and deva existence, is craving (taṇhā).
  4. The mind’s adhering to and tightly grasping those existences and sense objects is clinging (upādāna).
  5. Those wholesome or unwholesome volitions are called existence (bhava).

This is kamma-existence, that is, kamma. In insight contemplation, volition (cetanā) is taken as primary. In contemplating the causal relationship, the power of kamma (kammasatti), that is, kamma, is taken as primary.
v1-p15.V1-15-02: These five phenomena, formed or arisen when kamma-existence, kamma, was present in the previous life, are the causes of the five aggregates at rebirth-linking in this present life.54
v1-p15.V1-15-03: Of these five causes, ignorance, craving and clinging belong to the round of defilements. Formations and kamma belong to the round of kamma. These are the five past causes. Through them the following five present effects arise. They belong to the round of results.
v1-p15.V1-15-04:
Five Present Effects

Idha paṭisandhi viññāṇaṃ, okkanti nāmarūpaṃ, pasādo āyatanaṃ, phuṭṭho phasso, vedayitaṃ vedanā, ime pañca dhammā idhūpapattibhavasmiṃ purekatassa kammassa paccayā.

“Here, rebirth-linking is consciousness, descent is mentality and materiality, sensitivity is the base, touching is contact, and experiencing is feeling. These five phenomena in the present rebirth-existence occur with previously produced kamma as their condition.”54
v1-p15.V1-15-05:
In this present life:

  1. Rebirth-linking consciousness, or resultant consciousness, whose nature is to connect the past life with the present life, is consciousness (viññāṇa).
  2. The appearing that is like entering the mother’s womb is mentality and materiality (nāmarūpa).
  3. Sensitive matter, such as the sensitive matter of the eye, is the six bases (saḷāyatana).
  4. The meeting with and touching of the object is contact (phassa).
  5. The experiencing of the object that occurs as feeling the object is feeling (vedanā).
v1-p15.V1-15-06: Thus these five phenomena arise and are formed when there is birth (jāti), called rebirth-existence (upapattibhava), in this present life, supported and conditioned by kamma produced and accumulated in the previous life.54

v1-p16.V1-16-01:
Five Present Causes

Idha paripakkattā āyatanānaṃ moho avijjā, āyūhanā saṅkhārā, nikanti taṇhā, upagamanaṃ upādānaṃ, cetanā bhavoti ime pañca dhammā idha kammabhavasmiṃ āyatiṃ paṭisandhiyā paccayā.

“Here, with the maturing of the bases, delusion is ignorance, accumulation is formations, attachment is craving, approaching is clinging, and volition is existence. These five phenomena in the present kamma-existence are conditions for rebirth-linking in the future.”55
v1-p16.V1-16-02:
In this present life, with the maturing of the bases:

  1. Not knowing the four truths and wrongly perceiving a man, a woman, a person, a being, a human, a deity, a brahmā and so forth is ignorance (avijjā).
  2. The wholesome and unwholesome phenomena that produce the five aggregates, such as human existence with its human aggregates and deva existence with its deva aggregates, are formations (saṅkhārā).
  3. Attachment to and desire for those existences and sense objects, such as human and deva existence, is craving (taṇhā).
  4. The mind’s adhering to and tightly grasping those existences and sense objects is clinging (upādāna).
  5. Those wholesome or unwholesome volitions are called existence, kamma-existence, that is, kamma.

These five phenomena, when kamma-existence is present in this life, are causes of rebirth-linking in the future life.55
v1-p16.V1-16-03: Author’s note. In young children whose bases have not matured in this life, the mental process falls mostly into the life-continuum (bhavaṅga). Generally, they are not yet able to strive to produce kamma that generates another existence (bhavantarajanakakamma), kamma strong enough to bring forth a life. Hence the expression “with the maturing of the bases in this present life”.56
v1-p16.V1-16-04:
Five Future Effects

Āyatiṃ paṭisandhi viññāṇaṃ, okkanti nāmarūpaṃ, pasādo āyatanaṃ, phuṭṭho phasso, vedayitaṃ vedanā, ime pañca dhammā āyatiṃ upapattibhavasmiṃ idhakatassa kammassa paccayā.

“In the future, rebirth-linking is consciousness, descent is mentality and materiality, sensitivity is the base, touching is contact, and experiencing is feeling. These five phenomena in future rebirth-existence occur with kamma produced here as their condition.”57
v1-p16.V1-16-05:
1. Rebirth-linking consciousness, or resultant consciousness, whose nature is to connect the present life with the future life, is consciousness (viññāṇa).
  2. The appearing that is like entering the mother’s womb is mentality and materiality (nāmarūpa).
  3. Sensitive matter, such as the sensitive matter of the eye, is the six bases (saḷāyatana).
  4. The meeting with and touching of the object is contact (phassa).
  5. The experiencing of the object that occurs as feeling the object is feeling (vedanā).

These five phenomena arise when there is birth, called rebirth-existence, in the future life, supported and conditioned by kamma produced and accumulated in this present life.57
